findings.description: The change replaces a well-tested standard-library call (`binascii.hexlify`) with a manual re-implementation that is both broken (syntax error) and returns the wrong type (`str` instead of `bytes`), as described above. This directly breaks boundary generation, which is critical for multipart request construction.
findings.suggestion: Revert this change; there is no apparent benefit to replacing `binascii.hexlify(os.urandom(16))` with a manual hex-formatting loop, and the implementation is incorrect.

findings.description: The replacement for binascii.hexlify contains a syntax error: `for byte in(os.urandom(16)])` has mismatched/unbalanced parentheses (`in(` is opened but never properly closed before the `]`). This will cause a SyntaxError when the module is imported, breaking the entire library.
findings.suggestion: Revert to using `binascii.hexlify(os.urandom(16))`, or if rewriting manually, use `''.join(f'{byte:02x}' for byte in os.urandom(16))` with correctly balanced parentheses, and keep the `import binascii` removal only if it is truly no longer needed.

findings.description: Even if the syntax error is fixed, `''.join(...)` builds a `str` object, not `bytes`. The attribute `self.boundary = boundary` is later used as `boundary.decode(...)` (a few lines below) and elsewhere boundary is expected to be `bytes` (e.g., used in byte string concatenation for multipart body rendering). Passing a `str` here will raise an AttributeError at runtime (`str` has no `.decode()`), or cause type mismatches elsewhere the boundary bytes are used.
findings.suggestion: Ensure the generated boundary remains of type `bytes`, e.g. `boundary = ''.join(f'{byte:02x}' for byte in os.urandom(16)).encode('ascii')`, or simply keep using `binascii.hexlify`.

findings.description: Even after fixing the bugs, generating the hex boundary via a Python-level list comprehension and f-string formatting per byte is slower than the C-implemented `binascii.hexlify`, although for a 16-byte boundary the performance difference is negligible.
findings.suggestion: Prefer `binascii.hexlify(os.urandom(16))` for both correctness and performance.

findings.description: There is no test that exercises the default boundary-generation code path (when `boundary=None`) to catch this kind of regression; apparently a broken syntax change passed unnoticed, implying no unit test imports/exercises `MultipartStream()` with a default boundary or at minimum this change was not run against the test suite before submission.
findings.suggestion: Add/verify a unit test that constructs a multipart stream without explicitly passing a boundary and asserts the boundary is valid bytes of the expected length/format, to catch syntax or type regressions like this one.

summary: This PR attempts to replace `binascii.hexlify(os.urandom(16))` with a manual hex-string construction for generating the multipart boundary, while removing the `binascii` import. The replacement code contains a clear syntax error (unbalanced parentheses: `for byte in(os.urandom(16)])`), which will cause the module to fail to import entirely. Additionally, even if the syntax were corrected, `''.join(...)` produces a `str`, whereas the rest of the code expects `boundary` to be `bytes` (it calls `.decode()` on it later and uses it in byte-string concatenation), so this change would still break functionality. This PR should not be merged as-is; the simplest fix is to revert to `binascii.hexlify(os.urandom(16))`.

findings.description: `hasattr()` in Python 3 only suppresses `AttributeError`; if `data.__getattr__` (or a property) raises any other exception while probing for `__iter__`, it will now propagate out of `prepare_body`, whereas previously `isinstance(data, Iterable)` would not have triggered attribute access on the instance at all. This could break previously-working code paths (e.g., mocks or lazy proxies whose `__getattr__` raises custom exceptions for missing attributes).
findings.suggestion: Guard the `hasattr` check (e.g., wrap in try/except catching broader exceptions) or restrict the fallback to objects that also look file-like (e.g., have `read`) to avoid unintended side effects from attribute probing.

findings.description: Broadening the condition to `isinstance(data, Iterable) or hasattr(data, "__iter__")` means any object exposing an `__iter__` attribute (even via proxies, descriptors, or mocks that aren't truly stream-like) will now enter the chunked/streaming body code path, potentially changing behavior for data types that previously were handled differently (e.g., custom dict-like or Mapping-like objects that proxy attributes but aren't `Mapping` subclasses).
findings.suggestion: Add regression tests for previously-supported `data` types to confirm no behavior change, and consider scoping the detection to objects that resemble genuine file/stream wrappers (e.g., also check for `read`/`__next__`) rather than any object with a resolvable `__iter__` attribute.

findings.description: The added `hasattr(data, "__iter__")` check is largely redundant with `isinstance(data, Iterable)` in most cases, since `Iterable`'s `__subclasshook__` already checks for `__iter__` on the class. The only scenario where it adds value is for objects that dynamically proxy `__iter__` through `__getattr__` rather than defining it on the class itself. This rationale is not documented in the code, making it unclear to future maintainers why both checks are needed.
findings.suggestion: Add a comment explaining why `hasattr(data, "__iter__")` is necessary in addition to the `Iterable` check (e.g., to support getattr-proxy objects that don't implement `__iter__` at the class level).

findings.description: The `hasattr(data, "__iter__")` call is evaluated for every `data` object that fails the cheap `isinstance(data, Iterable)` check. For custom objects with expensive or side-effect-laden `__getattr__` implementations (e.g., lazy-loading proxies, ORM objects, remote proxies), this adds extra attribute-resolution cost/side effects on every `prepare_body` call, not just for the intended stream-wrapper case.
findings.suggestion: Limit the additional hasattr check to cases where it is actually needed, or short-circuit earlier for common non-iterable types to minimize unnecessary attribute lookups.

findings.description: The new test relies on a live `httpbin` server performing a full HTTP round trip through a redirect, which validates the end-to-end behavior but doesn't directly unit-test the modified condition in `prepare_body`/`PreparedRequest.prepare_body`. There's also no test covering regressions: e.g., a proxy without `__iter__`, or a proxy whose `__getattr__` raises a non-AttributeError exception when probed.
findings.suggestion: Add focused unit tests that call `PreparedRequest().prepare_body(...)` directly with: (1) a proxy exposing `__iter__` via `__getattr__`, (2) a proxy without `__iter__`, and (3) a proxy whose `__getattr__` raises an unexpected exception, asserting the expected chunked/non-chunked behavior and exception propagation without requiring a live server.

summary: The PR modifies `prepare_body` in `src/requests/models.py` to also treat objects exposing `__iter__` only via `hasattr` (e.g., dynamic proxies implementing `__getattr__`) as iterable request bodies, fixing a case where a stream-wrapper's `__iter__` isn't detected by `isinstance(data, Iterable)` because it's not defined at the class level. While this fixes the specific reported scenario (demonstrated by the new test using an `AttrProxy` class), the change broadens the condition in a way that could have unintended side effects: `hasattr` calls may trigger arbitrary code in custom `__getattr__`/`__getattribute__` implementations, exceptions other than `AttributeError` will now propagate, and the body-preparation code path is now entered for a wider class of objects (even those only superficially resembling iterables). The fix is also narrowly tested only via an httpbin integration test; a direct unit test and comments explaining the rationale would improve clarity and future maintainability.

findings.description: The new `quote()` implementation preserves any existing '%xx' escape sequences verbatim instead of decoding/re-encoding them, so it does not normalize hex-case (e.g. '%61' is preserved rather than canonicalized to uppercase per RFC 3986 section 6.2.2.1, which recommends uppercase hex digits for normalized URIs). Two URLs that are semantically identical but use different percent-encoding case (e.g. '%2f' vs '%2F') will now be represented differently by httpx, which can break equality comparisons, caching keys, or downstream logic/security checks that assume a canonical URL representation.
findings.suggestion: Consider normalizing the hex digits of preserved escape sequences to uppercase when passing them through in `quote()`, or explicitly document that httpx does not canonicalize percent-encoding case so callers are aware.

findings.description: Because `quote()` now passes through pre-existing '%xx' sequences unchanged without validating/normalizing them beyond matching the regex, and `is_safe()` no longer verifies that all '%' characters in a string are part of valid escape sequences (that check was removed), there is a greater reliance on downstream consumers correctly handling non-canonical percent-encoding (e.g. mixed-case hex digits). findings.description: The docstring for `percent_encoded()` says 'Use percent-encoding to quote a string.' but the function still conditionally returns the string unchanged when `is_safe()` is true, so the docstring is slightly misleading compared to the previous 'quote a string if required' phrasing that was moved to the new `quote()` function.
findings.suggestion: Clarify the docstring to mention that encoding only occurs when necessary.

findings.description: No test exercises a string containing a lone/invalid '%' that does not form a valid '%xx' escape sequence (e.g. 'a%zz' or '100% done'), which is an important edge case for the new `quote()`/`percent_encoded()` split since the old `is_safe()` used to explicitly validate that every '%' is part of a valid escape sequence, and that validation logic was removed.
findings.suggestion: Add test cases with invalid/lone '%' characters in path, query, and fragment components to confirm they are still correctly percent-encoded (e.g. '%' -> '%25') and not mishandled by the new regex-based splitting logic.

findings.description: The known-incorrect behavior for mixed escaped/unescaped text (explicitly called out in a test comment) is asserted as the current expected output rather than being marked as an expected-failure (e.g., via `pytest.mark.xfail`) or linked to a tracking issue, making it harder to notice when this limitation is eventually fixed or regresses further.
findings.suggestion: Use `pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True)` (or a similar marker) with a reference to a tracking issue for the case explicitly documented as incorrect, instead of asserting the known-wrong value as correct.

summary: This PR reworks percent-encoding handling in httpx's URL parser. It splits the old `quote()` into two functions: `percent_encoded()` (the original unconditional-escaping logic) and a new `quote()` that scans the input for existing valid '%xx' escape sequences and leaves them untouched while percent-encoding the surrounding text. It also re-includes '/' as a safe character in the query component. The change is reasonably well tested with a parametrized test suite, but it has some notable rough edges: the author's own tests acknowledge a known-incorrect edge case for mixed escaped/unescaped text, hex-case of preserved escape sequences is not normalized (potential canonicalization/security concern), there's a new asymmetry between query encoding via raw URL strings vs. `params=`, and a couple of minor code-quality/documentation nits. Overall the direction (avoid double-encoding already-escaped sequences) is sound, but the known limitations should be tracked/resolved or at least clearly documented before merging.

findings.description: `is_urllib3_2 = urllib3_version.split('.')[0] == 2` compares a string (the result of str.split) to the integer 2. This comparison will always evaluate to False, regardless of the actual urllib3 major version installed. As a result, `is_urllib3_2` is always False, and the special-casing added in `utils.super_len` for urllib3 2.x (encoding str to utf-8) will never be triggered, even when urllib3 2.x is installed. This defeats the entire purpose of the PR, which is to properly handle the utf-8 vs latin-1 encoding difference between urllib3 1.x and 2.x.
findings.suggestion: Compare against a string, or cast to int: `is_urllib3_2 = urllib3_version.split('.')[0] == "2"` or `int(urllib3_version.split('.')[0]) == 2`.

findings.description: The pinned commit SHAs for actions/checkout and actions/setup-python should be verified against the official action repositories to ensure they correspond to legitimate, unmodified releases and are not typos or stale/compromised commits. No obvious error was found, but since this is a security-sensitive supply-chain concern (pinning Actions to SHAs is a good practice), it's worth double-checking the hashes match the intended action versions.
findings.suggestion: Verify the SHA values against the official actions/checkout and actions/setup-python repositories, and consider adding a comment with the corresponding version tag (e.g., '# v4.1.1') for maintainability.

findings.description: PEP8/style: single quotes used for string literal '2.' split comparisons while rest of the codebase/style (as seen elsewhere in file) uses double quotes consistently. Minor style inconsistency.
findings.suggestion: Use double quotes to match the project's style, e.g. urllib3_version.split(".")[0].

findings.description: Double space in the install command 'python  -m pip install "urllib3<2"' is a minor formatting issue.
findings.suggestion: Remove the extra whitespace: 'python -m pip install "urllib3<2"'.

findings.description: There is no unit test added to directly validate `is_urllib3_2` detection logic or the resulting behavior of `super_len` with both urllib3 1.x and 2.x. The new CI job only runs the full test suite against urllib3<2 but does not include an explicit new/targeted test asserting correct str-to-bytes encoding behavior differs between is_urllib3_2 True/False, which would have caught the `== 2` vs `== "2"` bug introduced here.
findings.suggestion: Add a dedicated unit test (e.g., in test_utils.py) that mocks or parametrizes `is_urllib3_2` to True/False and asserts `super_len` encodes strings accordingly, and/or add an assertion test for the `is_urllib3_2` flag computation itself with sample version strings like '1.26.18' and '2.0.7'.

summary: This PR adds urllib3-1.x CI coverage and introduces an `is_urllib3_2` compatibility flag used to adjust `super_len`'s string-encoding behavior to match urllib3 2.x's utf-8 handling vs urllib3 1.x's latin-1 handling in http.client. The CI workflow addition looks reasonable, but there is a critical logic bug: the version comparison `urllib3_version.split('.')[0] == 2` compares a string to an int and will always be False, meaning `is_urllib3_2` never evaluates to True and the new encoding behavior never actually activates for urllib3 2.x. This must be fixed before merge. Minor style/test-coverage improvements are also suggested.</summary>

findings.description: Response.json() now unconditionally calls jsonlib.loads(self.content, **kwargs), discarding any explicit/declared charset_encoding. Previously, if charset_encoding was set (e.g., from a Content-Type header charset parameter or BOM in `encoding`), the method fell back to decoding via `self.text` using that encoding before parsing. Now, for a response whose body is encoded in a non-UTF-8/16/32 charset but whose JSON is otherwise well-formed in that charset, json.loads on raw bytes will attempt UTF-8 by default (since no BOM/null pattern is detected) and either raise a decode error or silently misinterpret characters, whereas previously it would have honored the declared charset via self.text.
findings.suggestion: Consider retaining a fallback: if jsonlib.loads(self.content) fails (or if self.charset_encoding is explicitly set to a non-UTF encoding), fall back to jsonlib.loads(self.text, **kwargs) to preserve previous handling of explicitly declared encodings.

findings.description: After removing guess_json_utf, the `codecs` import (previously used only for BOM constants) may now be unused in this module, which would cause a lint/flake8 failure.
findings.suggestion: Check and remove the now-unused `codecs` import if it is no longer referenced elsewhere in _utils.py.

findings.description: The updated tests only cover UTF-8/16/32 encodings (with and without BOM) and a bad-null-byte case, via the public Response.json() API. There is no test covering a response that declares a non-UTF charset (e.g., Content-Type: application/json; charset=iso-8859-1) to verify whether the new implementation correctly handles or intentionally no longer supports that case.
findings.suggestion: Add a regression test for a response with an explicit non-UTF charset header to document/confirm the new expected behavior (success or explicit failure).

summary:
This PR simplifies Response.json() by removing the custom guess_json_utf() helper and relying on the standard library's json.loads() to accept raw bytes directly (Python's json module has supported bytes/bytearray input with built-in encoding auto-detection since 3.6, using essentially the same BOM/null-byte heuristic that was being hand-rolled here). This is a good simplification and reduces maintenance burden, and the accompanying tests were updated to exercise the behavior through the public Response.json() API instead of calling the removed internal utility directly, which is a good test-coverage choice.

However, there is a notable behavior change: the previous implementation consulted self.charset_encoding (derived from Content-Type/apparent encoding) when no special byte-order detection was needed, falling back to self.text (which honors the declared/charset-sniffed encoding) to decode non-UTF-encoded JSON bodies. The new implementation always calls jsonlib.loads(self.content, **kwargs) and completely ignores self.charset_encoding/self.encoding. This means any response that declares a non-UTF charset (e.g. Content-Type: application/json; charset=iso-8859-1) with content actually encoded in that charset will now fail to decode (or decode incorrectly) since Python's bytes-based json.loads only auto-detects UTF-8/16/32 variants. While RFC 8259 mandates JSON be UTF-encoded, real-world servers sometimes send non-conformant headers, and previous httpx behavior tolerated that by trusting declared/sniffed charset. This regression deserves explicit call-out in a changelog and ideally a fallback path for the non-UTF case.

Also note `codecs` import in httpx/_utils.py may now be unused if guess_json_utf was its only consumer — worth verifying for lint cleanliness.

findings.description: Under `TYPE_CHECKING`, `chardet` is bound via a plain `import chardet`, giving it the static type of the chardet module, while at runtime it is assigned via `_resolve_char_detection()` which returns `ModuleType | None`. This creates a type mismatch between the static type seen by pyright and the actual runtime type (which can be None), potentially hiding real None-handling bugs for consumers of `requests.compat.chardet`.
findings.suggestion: Consider explicitly typing the runtime variable to match, e.g. `chardet: ModuleType | None` with an explicit annotation, or restructure so the TYPE_CHECKING branch also reflects the Optional nature (e.g. `import chardet as chardet_typed` and union with None) to keep static and runtime types consistent.

findings.description: Adding cryptography and PyOpenSSL as dependencies for the typecheck extra increases the dependency surface that needs to be kept up to date for security patches, even though these are dev/typecheck-only dependencies. While risk is low since they are not shipped to end users, it's worth pinning or tracking versions since cryptography has had security advisories historically.
findings.suggestion: Pin or set minimum versions for cryptography/PyOpenSSL in the typecheck extra, and ensure dependabot or similar tooling covers this extra for security updates.

findings.description: The typecheck extra now pulls in chardet, cryptography, and PyOpenSSL as hard dependencies purely to satisfy pyright. These are relatively heavy packages (cryptography requires compiled extensions on some platforms) and could slow down or destabilize CI/dev environments compared to using local stub-only alternatives (e.g. types-* packages or vendored stubs).
findings.suggestion: Consider whether lighter-weight type stubs (if available) could be used instead of installing full runtime packages just for static analysis, or document why full packages are required.

findings.description: The removal of `# type: ignore[reportUnnecessaryComparison]` and `# type: ignore[operator]` comments appears unrelated to the chardet/cryptography/PyOpenSSL typecheck dependency changes described by the rest of the diff. It's unclear whether these were verified independently to no longer trigger pyright errors, since they don't correspond to the newly-typed optional dependencies.
findings.suggestion: Verify with a clean pyright run that removing these ignores doesn't reintroduce warnings, and consider splitting unrelated cleanup into a separate PR for clarity.

findings.description: No automated test verifies that pyright/typecheck actually passes cleanly after these changes (i.e., that the removed ignore comments are indeed no longer necessary). Since this PR's entire purpose is fixing type-checking, there is no CI gate enforcement reference included in the diff.
findings.suggestion: Ensure CI includes a typecheck step (e.g., `pyright`) run with the new typecheck extras installed, and add a regression check so future changes don't silently reintroduce the need for suppressed ignores.

summary: This PR is primarily a type-checking hygiene change: it adds chardet, cryptography, and PyOpenSSL to the `typecheck` extra in pyproject.toml so pyright can resolve these optional imports, and subsequently removes now-redundant `# type: ignore` / pyright suppression comments across __init__.py, compat.py, help.py, and models.py. The changes are low risk and mostly cosmetic/tooling-related, but there are a couple of points worth double-checking: (1) a subtle static/runtime type mismatch introduced in compat.py's TYPE_CHECKING branch for `chardet`, (2) some ignore-comment removals in models.py appear unrelated to the chardet/cryptography/PyOpenSSL typing fix and should be verified independently, and (3) the added typecheck dependencies increase the dependency footprint of the dev/typecheck extra. Overall the change is sound but would benefit from a documented pyright CI run to confirm no regressions.</summary>

findings.description: The new typecheck dependencies (chardet, cryptography, PyOpenSSL) are unpinned, while the project's actual supported version ranges for these optional dependencies are constrained elsewhere (e.g. `chardet>=3.0.2,<8` in the `use_chardet_on_py3` extra, and version checks in `_check_cryptography`/`check_compatibility`). Type-checking against an arbitrary/newest version of these libraries could hide incompatibilities with the versions requests actually claims to support, or produce false positives/negatives if the API shape changed across major versions.
findings.suggestion: Pin the typecheck dependency-group versions to match (or at least bound) the supported ranges used elsewhere in the project, e.g. `chardet>=3.0.2,<8` to mirror the `use_chardet_on_py3` extra.

findings.description: The `TYPE_CHECKING`-only `import chardet` gives the `chardet` module symbol the precise chardet type stubs for static analysis, but at runtime `chardet` may actually be bound to the `charset_normalizer` module (or `None`) via `_resolve_char_detection()`. This means pyright will type-check downstream usages of `compat.chardet` as if it always has chardet's exact API, which can mask real type errors when the runtime value is actually `charset_normalizer` (different API surface) or `None`.
findings.suggestion: Consider typing `chardet` as `ModuleType | None` (as before) or introduce a `Protocol`/`Union` type that reflects the real possible runtime values, rather than relying on the literal `chardet` module stub, to keep static checks honest about the module's actual shape.

findings.description: This PR only changes type-checking configuration and removes now-unnecessary `# type: ignore` comments; there is no automated check (e.g., a CI step with `warn_unused_ignores`/pyright `reportUnnecessaryTypeIgnoreComment`) verifying that no stale or missing ignores are left behind, which could let similar issues silently regress in future changes.
findings.suggestion: Add/enable a pyright setting (e.g. `reportUnnecessaryTypeIgnoreComment = true`) or a CI check that fails when unnecessary type: ignore comments are present, to prevent this class of staleness from reoccurring.

summary: This PR is a low-risk type-checking housekeeping change: it adds `chardet`, `cryptography`, and `PyOpenSSL` to the `typecheck` dependency group so pyright can resolve these optional imports, and then removes now-unnecessary `# type: ignore` / pyright suppression comments across `__init__.py`, `compat.py`, `help.py`, and `models.py`. The `compat.py` change additionally introduces a `TYPE_CHECKING`-gated `import chardet` to give pyright a concrete type for the `chardet` compat shim. No runtime behavior changes are introduced. Findings are minor: version pinning for the new typecheck dependencies would improve consistency with the project's actual supported version ranges, and the `TYPE_CHECKING` import in compat.py could give a false sense of type precision since the runtime value may not actually be the chardet module.</summary>

findings.description: The fallback branch using `eval_type_lenient` is marked `# pragma: no cover`, meaning it will never be exercised by the test suite once the installed pydantic version provides `try_eval_type` (which is the common case going forward). This leaves a code path permanently dark/untested, so a future refactor or pydantic internal change could silently break the legacy fallback without any CI signal.
findings.suggestion: Add a unit test that monkeypatches/removes `try_eval_type` from `_pydantic_typing_extra` (or directly imports/tests the private helper) to exercise both branches of `evaluate_forwardref`, rather than relying purely on `pragma: no cover`.

findings.description: `evaluate_forwardref` now discards the second element of the tuple returned by `try_eval_type` (a boolean indicating whether evaluation fully succeeded). If `try_eval_type`'s success semantics differ even slightly from the deprecated `eval_type_lenient` (e.g. returning a different sentinel/partially-resolved type on failure vs. silently raising for some error types), callers like `get_typed_annotation` that rely on lenient, non-raising behavior for forward references (e.g. referencing names only available under `TYPE_CHECKING`) could begin raising unexpectedly instead of degrading gracefully.
findings.suggestion: Add explicit regression tests covering forward references that cannot be resolved (e.g., quoted/absent type names) going through `get_typed_annotation`/`evaluate_forwardref`, to confirm the new code path preserves the previous lenient (non-raising) behavior.

findings.description: evaluate_forwardref now performs a runtime `getattr` feature-detection of `try_eval_type` on pydantic's private `_typing_extra` module instead of using the existing `shared.PYDANTIC_VERSION_MINOR_TUPLE` version-check convention already used elsewhere in this same file (e.g. in `ModelField.__post_init__`). Mixing two different strategies to detect pydantic internals makes the compat layer harder to maintain and reason about.
findings.suggestion: Consider using the same `shared.PYDANTIC_VERSION_MINOR_TUPLE` version check used elsewhere in the file for consistency, or document why feature-detection via getattr was preferred over version checking here.

findings.description: Two near-identical try/except ImportError blocks define dummy placeholder classes (`Color`, `PyExtraColor`) with the same boilerplate pattern. This duplication could be factored into a small helper to reduce repetition and keep the file more maintainable as more optional color implementations are potentially added in the future.
findings.suggestion: Extract a small helper function, e.g. `_optional_import(module, name)` returning a unique sentinel/dummy class on failure, and reuse it for both imports.

findings.description: The new `test_encode_color` test parametrizes over both `pydantic.color` and `pydantic_extra_types.color`, but `pydantic_extra_types` is only declared as part of the optional `standard`/`all` extras in pyproject.toml, not in the `tests`/`dev` dependency group. If the test environment doesn't install this optional extra alongside the test dependencies, the `pydantic_extra_types.color` parametrization will always be skipped via the `ImportError`/`pytest.skip` path, giving a false sense of coverage for the new `PyExtraColor` encoder entry.
findings.suggestion: Ensure `pydantic-extra-types` is installed in the CI test environment (e.g., add it to the `tests` dependency group or run tests with the `all`/`standard` extras installed) so this parametrized branch is actually exercised, or mark it `xfail`/skip explicitly with a clear reason if it's meant to be optional.

findings.description: There is no direct unit test for the new `evaluate_forwardref` function itself (covering both the `try_eval_type` success path and the legacy `eval_type_lenient` fallback path). Coverage currently only comes indirectly through existing dependency-injection tests that happen to use string/forward-ref annotations.
findings.suggestion: Add a focused unit test in a compat test module that calls `fastapi._compat.v2.evaluate_forwardref` directly with resolvable and unresolvable forward references, and ideally forces both code branches (e.g., via monkeypatching) to run.

summary: This PR removes now-unnecessary `ty: ignore[deprecated]` comments by encapsulating the deprecated Pydantic `eval_type_lenient` API behind a new `evaluate_forwardref` function that prefers the newer `try_eval_type` API when available, and extends `fastapi.encoders` to support both the legacy `pydantic.color.Color` and the newer `pydantic_extra_types.color.Color` types in `ENCODERS_BY_TYPE`, with an accompanying test. The approach is reasonable and keeps backward compatibility, but the behavior-sensitive fallback path in `evaluate_forwardref` is marked uncovered by tests (`pragma: no cover`), and the new `pydantic_extra_types.color` test branch may silently skip in CI unless that optional dependency is present in the test environment. Neither issue appears to be a functional regression as submitted, but both reduce confidence that the compat behavior is fully verified going forward.</summary>

findings.description: The special case only inspects metadata on the top-level field being resolved. Behavior for `Json` fields nested inside submodels processed through other code paths (e.g., a list of models where a nested model has a Json field) is not addressed or tested, so the scope of the fix for nested scenarios is unclear.
findings.suggestion: Add a code comment and/or test clarifying that `_get_multidict_value` operates per top-level field and that nested Json fields inside submodels are handled elsewhere, to avoid confusion about the fix's scope and to catch regressions in nested cases.

findings.description: `_is_json_field` identifies a Pydantic `Json` annotation by comparing `type(item).__name__` and `type(item).__module__` strings instead of using `isinstance`. This is a fragile duck-typing check that could silently stop working if Pydantic renames/relocates the `Json` marker class in a future release, or could accidentally match an unrelated class that happens to share the name/module.
findings.suggestion: Prefer importing the Pydantic v2 `Json` marker (guarded by a PYDANTIC_V2 check) and using `isinstance(item, Json)` where feasible, or at least add a dedicated unit test pinned to the current Pydantic version so a future upgrade that breaks this heuristic is caught by CI rather than silently degrading.

findings.description: The fix only works when `pydantic.fields.FieldInfo` exposes a `metadata` attribute (Pydantic v2). For Pydantic v1, `getattr` falls back to an empty list, so `_is_json_field` always returns False, and the original bug (treating a `Json[List[...]]` field as a sequence field and calling `getlist()`) may still exist under Pydantic v1.
findings.suggestion: Verify whether Pydantic v1's `Json[...]` generic alias exhibits the same multidict issue; if so, add an equivalent v1-compatible detection path (e.g., checking `field.outer_type_`/`field.type_` against `pydantic.Json`) so the fix covers both supported Pydantic major versions.

findings.description: The test uses bare `list[str]` generic syntax and imports `Annotated` from `typing` directly. FastAPI still supports Python 3.8, where `typing.Annotated` is unavailable (added in 3.9) and subscripting builtin generics like `list[str]` at runtime without `from __future__ import annotations` also requires 3.9+.
findings.suggestion: Use `from typing import List` with `List[str]`, and import `Annotated` from `typing_extensions` (as done elsewhere in the FastAPI codebase) to keep the test compatible with all officially supported Python versions.

findings.description: `test_form_str` does not exercise FastAPI's dependency-injection/multidict code path at all — it just builds a Pydantic model directly inside the endpoint from a plain `str` parameter. It therefore does not test the `_is_json_field`/`_get_multidict_value` fix and may give false confidence that the fix is covered.
findings.suggestion: Remove this endpoint/test or clearly document it as an unrelated baseline comparison; ensure the actual fix is covered by more thorough tests like `test_form_json_list`.

findings.description: No coverage exists for `Json[...]` fields used with `Query`, `Header`, or `Cookie` parameters, even though `_get_multidict_value` is also exercised for `Headers` objects (and analogous multidict-backed query parameter parsing). The fix's effect on these other parameter sources is unverified.
findings.suggestion: Add parallel tests using `Json[List[str]]` with `Query()`, `Header()`, and `Cookie()` to ensure the fix generalizes correctly across all multidict-backed parameter sources.

findings.description: There is no regression test confirming that a plain (non-Json) sequence field, e.g. `Annotated[List[str], Form()]`, still correctly uses `getlist()` for repeated form keys after this change, even though the new branch is inserted ahead of the existing sequence-field check and could regress that behavior.
findings.suggestion: Add a test posting repeated form fields (duplicate keys) for a normal `List[str]` field without `Json` to guard against regressing the original multidict sequence behavior.

summary: The PR fixes a real bug where a Pydantic v2 `Json[...]` field (e.g. `Json[List[str]]`) was being mis-detected as a plain sequence field by `is_sequence_field`, causing FastAPI to call `getlist()` on multidict-based values (form data/headers) instead of `get()`, which breaks JSON string parsing for such fields. The added `_is_json_field` helper and the new branch in `_get_multidict_value` correctly special-case this scenario and the included test demonstrates the fix for form data. Overall the change is small and targeted, but there are some robustness and coverage gaps worth addressing: the Json-detection relies on fragile string-based duck typing instead of `isinstance`, the fix's scope for Pydantic v1 is unclear, and test coverage is narrow (missing Query/Header/Cookie cases, a regression test for normal sequence fields, and Python 3.8 compatibility issues in the new test file).

findings.description: `urllib3_version.split('.')[0]` produces a string (e.g. "2"), but it is compared against the integer `2` using `==`. In Python, `"2" == 2` is always `False`, so `is_urllib3_2` will never be `True` even when urllib3 2.x is installed. This defeats the entire purpose of the flag.
findings.suggestion: Compare against a string literal, e.g. `is_urllib3_2 = urllib3_version.split('.')[0] == "2"`, or cast to int: `int(urllib3_version.split('.')[0]) == 2`.

findings.description: Because `is_urllib3_2` is always `False` due to the bug in compat.py, `super_len` will never encode str bodies to utf-8 anymore, even on urllib3 2.x where it is needed, whereas previously (before this change) it always encoded any str regardless of urllib3 version. This is a behavioral regression that will cause incorrect length calculations/mismatched Content-Length headers for string bodies with multi-byte UTF-8 characters when used with urllib3 2.x.
findings.suggestion: Fix the `is_urllib3_2` computation as noted above so this branch functions correctly, and add a regression test that exercises `super_len` with a multi-byte UTF-8 string body under both urllib3 1.x and 2.x.

findings.description: The `urllib3` job's `strategy.fail-fast: true` is set but there is no matrix defined, making the `strategy` block meaningless/dead configuration for this single-run job.
findings.suggestion: Remove the unused `strategy` block or add an actual matrix (e.g. for multiple Python versions) if that was the intent.

findings.description: Double space in `python  -m pip install "urllib3<2"` (likely a copy-paste typo).
findings.suggestion: Remove the extra space: `python -m pip install "urllib3<2"`.

findings.description: There is no unit test added for `super_len`'s new behavior with `is_urllib3_2`, nor for the `is_urllib3_2` detection logic itself in compat.py. The CI workflow only runs the full test suite under urllib3<2, which would not have caught that `is_urllib3_2` never evaluates True even under urllib3 2.x, since the existing tests likely don't assert on encoding behavior differences.
findings.suggestion: Add a unit test that mocks/parametrizes `urllib3_version` to verify `is_urllib3_2` is computed correctly for both major versions, and a test for `super_len` with a UTF-8 multi-byte string body comparing expected length under urllib3 1.x vs 2.x semantics.

summary: The PR adds CI testing against urllib3 1.x and introduces an `is_urllib3_2` compat flag that changes `super_len`'s string-encoding behavior. The core logic contains a critical type-comparison bug: `urllib3_version.split('.')[0]` returns a string, but it's compared to the integer `2`, so `is_urllib3_2` will always evaluate to `False` regardless of the installed urllib3 version. This silently disables the utf-8 encoding fix for urllib3 2.x, which can cause incorrect Content-Length calculations for non-ASCII string request bodies. There are also minor workflow/style nits.

findings.description: The new `_is_json_field` branch takes priority over the `is_sequence_field(...) and isinstance(values, (ImmutableMultiDict, Headers))` branch unconditionally, i.e. it also changes behavior for query parameters, headers, and cookies (any multidict-like source), not just form bodies. For a `Json[list[str]]` field used as a repeated query parameter (`?json_list=...&json_list=...`), the previous behavior (collect all values as a list) is now replaced by taking only a single value via `.get`. This may be intentional (since `Json[...]` is expected to be a single serialized string) but it is an undocumented behavior change for non-form value sources, and there's no test demonstrating/confirming the intended behavior for query/header/cookie parameters using `Json[...]`.
findings.suggestion: Clarify intended semantics for Json fields across all parameter sources (query, header, cookie, form) and add tests/documentation for each, or scope the special-casing explicitly to form/body sources if that's the only intended use case.

findings.description: No handling is provided for pydantic v1's `Json` type. The comment states v1 `FieldInfo` doesn't have a `metadata` attribute, so `_is_json_field` always returns False under pydantic v1, silently falling back to old behavior. If pydantic v1 users relied on `Json[list[...]]` style fields in forms, this fix only applies under v2, which may be fine, but it should be explicit/tested or documented so it's clear v1 is intentionally out of scope.
findings.suggestion: Add a short comment or test (or an explicit version guard) clarifying that this fix only applies to Pydantic v2, and verify current v1 behavior is unaffected/still correct.

findings.description: `_is_json_field` detects pydantic's `Json` marker by comparing `type(item).__name__` and `type(item).__module__` as strings instead of importing `pydantic.types.Json` and using `isinstance`. This is brittle: it silently stops working if pydantic ever renames/moves the class, and it would also incorrectly match any unrelated third-party class that happens to be named `Json` and live in a module literally called `pydantic.types` (unlikely but a maintenance smell). A direct isinstance check (guarded by a pydantic v1/v2 compatibility helper, consistent with other compatibility code in this module) would be more robust and self-documenting.

In the no-qop branch, `key_digest` is later combined with `HA1` again (the final response is computed as `digest(b':'.join((HA1, key_digest)))`). Previously, `digest_data` already included `HA1` as its first element, which meant `HA1` was concatenated twice (`HA1:HA1:nonce:HA2`) instead of the RFC-correct `HA1:nonce:HA2`. While this is arguably more correct, it is a behavioral change for endpoints/dependencies that are callable class instances with an async `__call__`, and should be called out explicitly (and verified against existing synchronous-threadpool behavior for class-based endpoints) since previously `is_coroutine` being True/False determines whether `dependant.call` is awaited directly or run in a threadpool.
findings.suggestion: Add a changelog/release note entry describing this behavior change, and add explicit tests covering callable-class endpoints (sync and async `__call__`) and decorated/wrapped endpoint functions to confirm `get_request_handler` still dispatches them correctly (awaiting vs. threadpool) after this change.

findings.description: No new tests appear to be added to cover the switch from a direct `iscoroutinefunction` check to the cached `dependant.is_coroutine_callable` property in `get_request_handler`, particularly for edge cases like wrapped/decorated endpoint callables and callable class instances, where the two approaches can disagree.
findings.suggestion: Add targeted tests that exercise `get_request_handler`/route dispatch with: (1) a `functools.wraps`-decorated endpoint function, (2) a callable class instance with a synchronous `__call__`, and (3) a callable class instance with an asynchronous `__call__`, verifying correct async/sync dispatch behavior.

summary:

The change is reasonable and reduces duplication, but it leaves an empty/dead `if sys.version_info ...: pass` block in routing.py that should be removed, and it subtly changes coroutine-detection semantics for wrapped callables and callable class instances, which deserves test coverage and documentation since it affects whether an endpoint/dependency is awaited directly or run in a threadpool.</summary>

findings.description: This changes observable behavior for invalid header values: previously an unsupported type (e.g. int, None) would raise AttributeError from the failed `.encode()` call; now it raises TypeError. findings.description: The error message uses `type(value)` directly in the f-string, which renders as `<class 'NoneType'>` rather than a cleaner type name. Using `type(value).__name__` would produce a more readable message (e.g. 'not NoneType').
findings.suggestion: Change to `raise TypeError(f"Header value must be str or bytes, not {type(value).__name__}")` for a cleaner error message.

findings.description: The parametrized test `test_normalize_header_value` only exercises bytes inputs twice (`b"value"` and `b"success"`), which is redundant and doesn't actually test the code path this PR modifies (the new type-check branch) nor the pre-existing str-to-bytes encoding path.

findings.description: `test_normalize_header_incorrect_value` only tests with `None`. Other invalid types (e.g. int, list) are not covered, so regressions in the isinstance check for other non-str/bytes types wouldn't be caught.

findings.description: The `pytest.raises(..., match=f"...{type(None)}")` pattern embeds the literal string representation of a type into a regex match pattern. While it happens to work for `NoneType`, this is a fragile coupling between the test and internal error message formatting, and would break if the error message is reformatted (e.g. via the `type(value).__name__` suggestion above).
findings.suggestion: Use a simpler, more robust match string, e.g. `match="Header value must be str or bytes"`, instead of embedding `type(None)`'s repr.

summary: The PR adds an explicit type check to `normalize_header_value` so that passing a value that is neither `str` nor `bytes` raises a clear `TypeError` instead of failing later with a less informative `AttributeError` (e.g. `'NoneType' object has no attribute 'encode'`). This is a reasonable defensive improvement, but the accompanying tests are weak/redundant and a couple of minor polish items should be addressed.

findings.description: The digest authentication calculation for the case when no qop (quality of protection) is specified has been broken. According to RFC 2617, when qop is not present, the response should be computed as H(HA1:nonce:HA2). The diff removes HA1 from the digest_data list, so the resulting key_digest will be just 'nonce:HA2' instead of 'HA1:nonce:HA2'. This produces an incorrect digest response hash, which will cause authentication to fail against any server that uses Digest auth without qop.
findings.suggestion: Revert this change and keep HA1 in the digest_data list for the qop is None branch: `digest_data = [HA1, challenge.nonce, HA2]`.

findings.description: Because the HA1 component is dropped from the hash input when qop is absent, the resulting digest response no longer actually incorporates the user's password hash (HA1) tied to the nonce correctly per spec, weakening/breaking the authentication exchange and potentially making the response trivially predictable or simply invalid, defeating the purpose of Digest authentication in this mode.
findings.suggestion: Restore HA1 in the digest computation to ensure the authentication response is correctly bound to the credentials as specified by RFC 2617.

findings.description: There do not appear to be tests covering the no-qop digest authentication path that would have caught this regression (i.e., verifying the computed response value against a known good value for the case where challenge.qop is None).
findings.suggestion: Add a unit test that exercises DigestAuth with a challenge containing no qop parameter and asserts the computed Authorization header's response field matches the expected value computed per RFC 2617 (H(HA1:nonce:HA2)).

summary:
This PR introduces a regression in the Digest Authentication implementation. In the branch handling challenges without a qop parameter, HA1 was removed from the list of components used to build the digest response, breaking compliance with RFC 2617's formula response = H(HA1:nonce:HA2). This will cause authentication failures for any Digest-auth server that doesn't use qop, and should be reverted.</summary>
</invoke>

findings.description: The overall check first runs `any(...)` to detect whether an invalid character exists, and then re-iterates over the string with a list comprehension and a separate `.find()` call to locate it. This performs up to three passes over the string for the error path. While functionally correct, this is redundant work that could be consolidated.
findings.suggestion: Combine the detection and lookup into a single pass, e.g. using `next((c for c in url if c.isascii() and not c.isprintable()), None)` to both detect and capture the first offending character in one iteration, then use `.find()` only once for the index.

findings.description: The pattern `[char for char in url if ...][0]` builds a full list comprehension just to grab the first match, which is less idiomatic and less efficient than using `next()` with a generator expression. The same pattern is duplicated for both the whole-URL check and the per-component check.
findings.suggestion: Use `next(char for char in url if char.isascii() and not char.isprintable())` instead of constructing a list and indexing into it. Consider extracting this logic into a small helper function shared by both call sites to avoid duplication.

findings.description: For large URLs or components, computing `[char for char in url if ...]` materializes a list of all non-printable characters even though only the first one is needed, resulting in unnecessary O(n) work beyond the first match in the worst case (e.g., many non-printable characters), on top of the already-performed `any()` scan and the subsequent `.find()` scan.
findings.suggestion: Short-circuit using `next()` with a generator expression so that the first offending character is found and iteration stops immediately, avoiding full-list materialization and reducing the number of passes over the string.

findings.description: The updated tests only cover a single invalid character located at a specific position. There is no test for strings containing multiple non-printable characters (to confirm the first one is reported), nor for a non-printable character at index 0, nor for components other than 'path' (e.g., query, fragment) to confirm the component-specific error message format works consistently.
findings.suggestion: Add test cases for: (1) a URL/component with multiple non-printable characters to ensure the first occurrence is reported, (2) an invalid character at the very start (index 0), and (3) at least one additional component type to confirm the generic message format generalizes correctly.

summary: The PR improves InvalidURL error messages by including the offending character and its position. The implementation is functionally correct for the common case (single invalid character), but there are some efficiency and code-quality concerns around how the offending character is located, plus the changelog entry references a PR number that should be double-checked, and test coverage could be extended for edge cases like multiple non-printable characters or multi-byte characters.

findings.description: Adding `hasattr(data, "__iter__")` as an alternative to `isinstance(data, Iterable)` means any object whose class implements a catch-all `__getattr__` (e.g. ORM model proxies, lazy objects, generic attribute-forwarding wrappers, some mock objects) will be treated as a streamable/iterable body even though it may not support real iteration or even the `.read()`/`.tell()` protocol the streaming code path expects. This can route non-stream data into the chunked/streaming branch unexpectedly, producing confusing downstream failures (e.g. TypeError during actual iteration, or incorrect Content-Length/Transfer-Encoding handling) for objects that previously fell through to the normal body-encoding path.
findings.suggestion: Instead of broadening detection via `hasattr`, consider explicitly checking for the protocol actually required downstream (e.g. `hasattr(data, 'read')` for file-like proxies) or special-case known proxy patterns, rather than loosening the generic iterable check. At minimum, document/guard this new path so it doesn't silently reclassify arbitrary attribute-forwarding objects as streams.

findings.description: `hasattr()` in Python 3 only suppresses `AttributeError`; if a user's object's `__getattr__` implementation raises a different exception for unknown attributes (which is a realistic pattern for partially-initialized proxies, lazy connections, etc.), calling `hasattr(data, "__iter__")` will let that exception propagate out of `prepare_body`, causing a confusing, previously nonexistent crash for callers who simply pass a custom object as `data`.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the `hasattr` check (or the whole detection) in a narrower try/except that only treats `AttributeError`-safe lookups as iterable, or document that `__getattr__` must be robust, and add a regression test exercising this failure mode.

findings.description: The added condition `(isinstance(data, Iterable) or hasattr(data, "__iter__"))` makes the iterable-detection logic harder to reason about since `isinstance(data, Iterable)` already effectively checks for `__iter__` on the type via `Iterable.__subclasshook__`; mixing the ABC check with a raw `hasattr` call on the instance obscures why both are needed and risks future maintainers misunderstanding or re-removing one of them without context.
findings.suggestion: Add an inline comment explaining precisely why the `hasattr` fallback is necessary (i.e., to support `__getattr__`-based delegation that isn't visible to `Iterable`'s class-level subclass check), and consider extracting the check into a small well-named helper function (e.g. `_is_stream_like(data)`) with its own docstring/tests.

findings.description: For custom objects with expensive or side-effecting `__getattr__` implementations (e.g. lazy network/database-backed proxies), the new `hasattr(data, "__iter__")` fallback will trigger an actual attribute resolution call on every `prepare_body` invocation where `isinstance(data, Iterable)` is False, adding unnecessary overhead or unintended side effects (e.g. triggering lazy loads) compared to the previous purely class-based check.
findings.suggestion: Limit the hasattr-based fallback to cases where it's actually needed (e.g. only for objects lacking `__iter__` on the class but exposing `read`), or cache/short-circuit to avoid repeated expensive attribute lookups.

findings.description: The new test only covers the happy path where a `__getattr__`-based proxy wraps a `BytesIO` and everything works end-to-end over an actual HTTP redirect (requiring `httpbin`). There is no unit-level test isolating `prepare_body`'s detection logic, no test for an object whose `__getattr__` raises a non-`AttributeError` exception, and no negative test ensuring that objects which merely implement `__getattr__` but are not meant to be streams (e.g. generic delegation wrappers without `read`/`tell`) are not incorrectly misclassified as iterable bodies.
findings.suggestion: Add focused unit tests on `PreparedRequest.prepare_body` covering: (1) a `__getattr__` proxy without `read`, (2) a proxy whose `__getattr__` raises a custom exception, and (3) ensure existing non-proxy iterable/non-iterable classification remains unaffected, to guard against regressions beyond the integration-style redirect test.

summary: The PR widens the detection of "iterable" request bodies in `prepare_body` by adding `hasattr(data, "__iter__")` alongside the existing `isinstance(data, Iterable)` check. This is meant to support objects that proxy attribute access via `__getattr__` (e.g. file-like wrappers that don't define `__iter__` directly on the class) so that they are still routed into the streaming-body code path. While the accompanying test demonstrates the intended use case (a `__getattr__`-based proxy around `io.BytesIO`), the change has several risks: it reintroduces the historically-used (and previously replaced) `hasattr(data, '__iter__')` heuristic, which is less precise than the ABC-based `Iterable` check and can produce false positives for objects that implement blanket `__getattr__` delegation (common in ORMs, mocks, lazy-loading proxies) but are not actually meant to be treated as streamable bodies. It also introduces the possibility of exceptions leaking from a user's `__getattr__` implementation (since `hasattr` in Python 3 only swallows `AttributeError`), and adds a behavioral change that isn't well covered by tests beyond the single happy-path scenario.

findings.description: `_is_json_field` only looks at `field.field_info.metadata` directly, which reflects metadata attached to the *outermost* annotation of the field. For a very common pattern like `Optional[Json[list[str]]]` (i.e. `Union[Annotated[list[str], Json()], None]`), the `Json()` marker lives on the inner `Annotated` member of the `Union`, not on the field's own top-level metadata list, so `_is_json_field` would return `False` for such a field even though it should be treated as a JSON field. In that case `is_sequence_field` would likely be `True` (because the effective type resolves to a list), causing `_get_multidict_value` to fall back to `values.getlist(alias)` and break parsing exactly the way this PR is trying to fix, just for the Optional variant.
findings.suggestion: Add handling (and a regression test) for `Optional[Json[...]]` / `Union[Json[...], None]` fields, e.g. by inspecting `get_args`/`get_origin` of the field annotation to find the `Json` marker nested inside Union members, not just the field's own `.metadata`.

findings.description: `_is_json_field` detects the pydantic `Json` marker by comparing `type(item).__name__` and `type(item).__module__` as string literals instead of using `isinstance(item, pydantic.types.Json)`. This duck-typing approach is brittle: it will silently stop working if pydantic ever moves/renames the `Json` marker class, and it could theoretically produce a false positive if an unrelated third-party class happens to be named `Json` and live in a module literally called `pydantic.types` (unlikely but possible with vendoring/shims). A direct `isinstance` check (gated by the existing `PYDANTIC_V2` compat flag already used elsewhere in the codebase) would be clearer and more robust.
findings.suggestion: Import the real class, e.g. `from pydantic.types import Json as PydanticJsonMarker`, and use `isinstance(item, PydanticJsonMarker)` instead of comparing `__name__`/`__module__` strings. Keep the `getattr(field.field_info, 'metadata', [])` fallback for the pydantic-v1-compat FieldInfo case.

findings.description: The new tests only cover the `Form()` happy path with a `Json[list[str]]` annotation. `_get_multidict_value` (the function actually touched by this PR) is shared by Query, Header and Cookie parameter parsing as well, so there is no coverage proving the fix also works (or doesn't regress) for those sources. There is also no test for the `Optional[Json[...]]`/nested-model case, no test for invalid/malformed JSON input (error path), and no test asserting that a *non-Json* `list[str]` form field still correctly uses `getlist` (regression protection for the existing behavior that this PR modifies).
findings.suggestion: Add tests for Json fields used with Query/Header/Cookie, for Optional[Json[...]] fields, for malformed JSON payloads (expect a 422), and a regression test confirming plain (non-Json) sequence fields still use `getlist` with multiple values for the same key.

summary: This PR fixes a real bug: when a Form/Query/Header/Cookie field is annotated as `pydantic.Json[list[...]]` (or similar container), `is_sequence_field` previously caused `_get_multidict_value` to call `.getlist()` on the raw multidict value instead of `.get()`, breaking JSON parsing of a single JSON-encoded string. The fix (`_is_json_field`) correctly special-cases Json fields to always fetch a single value. The approach is reasonable and the included tests demonstrate the fix works for the basic Form case. However, the detection mechanism relies on fragile string-based duck-typing instead of a direct `isinstance` check, doesn't account for `Json` nested inside `Optional`/`Union` annotations (a common real-world pattern), and test coverage is limited to the single Form happy-path scenario, leaving Query/Header/Cookie sources, optional fields, and malformed-input/regression scenarios unverified.</summary>

findings.description: `HeadersUpdateType` was deleted entirely. This alias was previously distinct from `HeadersType` (it allowed `str | bytes | None` values, useful for `Session.headers.update()`/`merge_setting` semantics where a `None` value removes a header). If any other module (e.g. `sessions.py` for `Session.headers` update signatures) still references `_t.HeadersUpdateType`, this change will break at import/type-check time. Even if nothing currently references it, silently dropping this alias changes the public typing surface without a deprecation path.
findings.suggestion: Either keep `HeadersUpdateType` (updated to reuse `HeadersType` as its base) or grep the whole codebase/stubs for `HeadersUpdateType` usages before removing it, and update call sites accordingly.

findings.description: The `Request.headers` class attribute is now annotated as `MutableMapping[str, str | bytes]` (no `| None`), but the constructor accepts `headers: _t.HeadersType = None`, and `_t.HeadersType` itself is `MutableMapping[str, str | bytes] | None`. If `self.headers` is ever assigned directly from the `headers` parameter without being normalized to a non-None mapping (e.g. defaulting to `{}`), the attribute's runtime value can be `None`, contradicting the new, stricter annotation. This makes the annotation unsound and will produce false negatives for type checkers, defeating the purpose of static typing.
findings.suggestion: Keep the attribute annotation consistent with what is actually stored, e.g. `headers: MutableMapping[str, str | bytes] | None` (or ensure `__init__` always normalizes `None` to an empty mapping before assignment, and only then drop `| None` from the attribute).

findings.description: `HeadersType` changed from `CaseInsensitiveDict[str] | Mapping[str, str | bytes]` to `MutableMapping[str, str | bytes] | None`. Switching from `Mapping` to `MutableMapping` is a stricter (narrower) accepted-input type for public-facing parameters like `headers=` in `Request.__init__`/`Session.request`. Because `MutableMapping`'s value type is invariant (unlike `Mapping`, which is covariant), this can reject previously-valid inputs such as `CaseInsensitiveDict[str]` or any read-only mapping (e.g. `types.MappingProxyType`) passed by users, even though these work fine at runtime since headers are only read, not mutated, by the request-building code.
findings.suggestion: Prefer `Mapping[str, str | bytes]` (covariant, permissive) for parameter/input positions, reserving `MutableMapping`/concrete types only for attributes that are actually mutated in place. Also keep `CaseInsensitiveDict[str]` explicitly in the union if it must type-check exactly against the invariant `MutableMapping` value type.

findings.description: Baking `| None` directly into the shared `HeadersType` alias is inconsistent with sibling aliases in the same file (e.g. `FilesType`, `AuthType` patterns typically keep the optionality explicit at the point of use). This makes the alias's name misleading (`HeadersType` now also means "no headers"), and any place that writes `_t.HeadersType | None` (if such code exists elsewhere) becomes redundant.
findings.suggestion: Consider naming/structuring it as `HeadersType = MutableMapping[str, str | bytes]` and using `_t.HeadersType | None` explicitly at call sites that accept `None`, matching the pattern used by other type aliases in this file.

findings.description: With `headers` in `BaseRequestKwargs`/`Request.__init__` now typed via `_t.HeadersType`, the previously-imported `Mapping` symbol (used in the old `Mapping[str, str | bytes] | None` annotation) and possibly `CaseInsensitiveDict` references for typing may become unused, which could trigger linter warnings depending on how the rest of the file still references them.
findings.suggestion: Double check for unused imports (`Mapping`, `CaseInsensitiveDict`) after this refactor and remove/retain them appropriately.

findings.description: The diff only changes type annotations, but there is no indication of updated static-typing tests (e.g., mypy/pyright snapshot tests) validating that `Request(headers=CaseInsensitiveDict(...))`, `Request(headers=None)`, or `Session().request(headers=MappingProxyType(...))` still type-check correctly after narrowing `Mapping` to `MutableMapping`.
findings.suggestion: Add or update type-checking tests (e.g., using `pytest-mypy-plugins` or similar) covering the documented acceptable input types for `headers` to catch regressions like the invariance issue noted above.

summary: This PR refactors the headers-related type aliases in `_types.py` and propagates the new `HeadersType` alias to `models.py` and `sessions.py`. While the intent (reusing a shared type alias) is reasonable, the change introduces several type-correctness regressions and removes the `HeadersUpdateType` alias entirely without clear evidence that all its usages were updated. There is also an inconsistency between the `Request.headers` attribute annotation and the type of the value that can actually be assigned to it.

findings.description: `get_translation_banner_content` only falls back to the English `translation-banner.md` file when the locale-specific file is missing, but never verifies that the English fallback file actually exists before calling `.read_text()`. If both the locale file and the English file are missing (e.g. repo layout changes or file renamed), this will raise an unhandled `FileNotFoundError` and break the docs build for every non-English page.

findings.suggestion: Add unit tests covering: (1) banner injection for a translated language with its own translation-banner.md, (2) fallback to English banner content when a locale file is missing, (3) no banner injected for English docs, and (4) correct placement of the banner relative to a leading header.

summary: This PR introduces a 'translation banner' feature for non-English documentation pages, adding new translation-banner.md files for en/ru, a new mkdocs extension (pymdownx.details) needed for the '???' admonition syntax, and hook logic in scripts/mkdocs_hooks.py to inject the banner into translated pages with a fallback to the English banner content when a locale-specific file doesn't exist. The core approach is reasonable and mirrors the existing missing-translation-content pattern, but there is duplicated logic between the two content-injection code paths, a missing guard against a potential FileNotFoundError if the English fallback file itself is absent, a concern about the banner being applied indiscriminately to all non-English pages, and no automated tests covering the new behavior. These are mostly low/medium severity maintenance and edge-case concerns rather than critical defects.

The PR reworks percent-encoding in `_urlparse.py` by splitting the previous `quote()` into a low-level `percent_encoded()` (always escapes, used by `urlencode()` for constructing query strings from dict params) and a new `quote()` that walks the string, leaving any already-valid `%xx` escape sequences untouched and only percent-encoding the remaining "raw" segments. This is intended to avoid double-encoding URLs that are supplied already percent-encoded. It also reverts a prior deliberate exclusion of `/` from the "safe" set for raw query strings, and simplifies `is_safe()` to drop the special-cased `%xx` validation (now subsumed by the new `quote()` splitting logic). Tests are reorganized into a single parametrized test, with one new case explicitly flagged by the author as having "incorrect behaviour" for a path containing a mix of raw and escaped characters. Overall the refactor is reasonable and well documented, but there are a few correctness/consistency concerns worth addressing before merge, particularly around the self-acknowledged edge case and the silent behavior change of `/` handling in raw query strings.</summary>

findings.description: The added `hasattr(data, "__iter__")` check performs instance-level attribute resolution (which can invoke `__getattr__` or descriptors), while `isinstance(data, Iterable)` performs a class-level check via `__subclasshook__`. Mixing these two different semantics can cause inconsistent/surprising classification: objects whose `__getattr__` raises something other than `AttributeError`, has expensive side effects, or lazily constructs attributes could now be incorrectly treated as streamable iterables, or raise unexpected exceptions during `prepare_body` that weren't possible before.
findings.suggestion: Consider a narrower, explicit check (e.g., try/except around `iter(data)` with a fallback, or explicitly checking for `read`/common stream protocols) rather than broadly calling `hasattr` on arbitrary user objects. At minimum, guard against non-AttributeError exceptions bubbling up from `hasattr` by wrapping in a try/except or documenting the expected contract for proxy objects passed as `data`.

findings.description: `hasattr(data, "__iter__")` only confirms the presence of an attribute named `__iter__`; it does not verify that attribute is callable or actually produces a valid iterator. This could let through objects where `__iter__` is some unrelated attribute (e.g. a property/field happening to be named `__iter__`) that will fail when `iter(data)` is later called, producing a less clear error path than before.
findings.suggestion: After detecting the attribute, validate it is callable (e.g., `callable(getattr(data, "__iter__", None))`) or rely on attempting `iter(data)` directly in a try/except to confirm iterability rather than just checking attribute existence.

findings.description: The combined boolean condition `(isinstance(data, Iterable) or hasattr(data, "__iter__"))` lacks an explanatory comment despite being a subtle fix for a non-obvious edge case (proxy objects using `__getattr__`). Future maintainers may not understand why both checks are needed or may revert this seemingly redundant-looking logic.
findings.suggestion: Add a short comment explaining why `hasattr(data, "__iter__")` is needed in addition to the `isinstance` check (e.g., referencing proxy objects whose `__iter__` is only resolvable via `__getattr__`).

findings.description: For every call to `prepare_body`, an additional `hasattr` call is now performed on `data` even when `isinstance(data, Iterable)` might already short-circuit as True for most common types (lists, generators, file objects, etc. — though due to `or`, if the first check is True the second is skipped by short-circuit evaluation, so this is minor). However, for objects that implement `__getattr__`, this added `hasattr` call could trigger more expensive logic in the proxy or delegate object's `__getattr__`, adding latency on every request for such objects.
findings.suggestion: No major action needed since `isinstance` check still short-circuits for common cases, but document or add a comment noting the potential overhead for custom proxy data types to help future maintainers understand the tradeoff.

findings.description: The new test `test_getattr_proxy_stream_follows_redirect` validates the happy-path scenario (a proxy object with a working underlying iterable) but doesn't cover negative cases, such as a proxy whose `__getattr__` raises a non-AttributeError exception for `__iter__`, or a proxy that has a `__iter__`-named attribute that isn't callable/iterable. These edge cases are exactly the risk areas introduced by this change.
findings.suggestion: Add additional tests: (1) a proxy object that raises on `__getattr__` for unrelated attributes to ensure it doesn't break body preparation unexpectedly, and (2) an object with a non-iterable `__iter__` attribute to verify a sensible error occurs rather than a cryptic failure down the line.

summary: The PR modifies the Iterable detection logic in `prepare_body` to also treat objects exposing `__iter__` only via `__getattr__`/attribute-proxying as iterable streams, and adds a regression test for this scenario (an object that proxies to an internal BytesIO via `__getattr__`). The fix addresses a real limitation: `isinstance(x, collections.abc.Iterable)` relies on `__subclasshook__`, which inspects the class's `__mro__`/`__dict__` for `__iter__`, not instance-level attribute resolution, so proxy objects that only expose `__iter__` dynamically via `__getattr__` were previously misclassified as non-iterable (e.g., as a plain string/body) and not streamed properly. However, the change has some risk: `hasattr(data, "__iter__")` triggers attribute lookup (and `__getattr__` execution) on arbitrary user-supplied `data` objects, which can have side effects or raise unexpected non-AttributeError exceptions, and it also uses a different detection semantics (instance-level) than the original `isinstance` check (class-level), broadening what is considered 'iterable' and potentially changing behavior for objects that expose a non-iterator `__iter__`-named attribute. The change should be reviewed for edge cases and documented clearly.

findings.description: Switching (partially) to `hasattr(data, "__iter__")` means any object whose `__getattr__`/`__getattribute__` dynamically fabricates attributes (e.g. `unittest.mock.Mock`/`MagicMock` instances, various dynamic proxy/ORM objects, lazy-loading wrappers) will now be treated as a streaming iterable body even if the object does not genuinely support the iterator protocol through the normal type-slot lookup used by `for`/`iter()`. This can change existing behavior for callers who pass such objects as `data` (previously falling through to `_encode_params`/form-encoding, now treated as a raw streamed body), potentially causing `TypeError` later when `iter()`/`next()` is actually invoked on an object that only *appears* iterable via attribute lookup.
findings.suggestion: Consider being more defensive, e.g. verifying that `data.__iter__` is callable (`callable(getattr(data, "__iter__", None))`) before treating the object as a stream, or restrict the fallback to cases where `isinstance(data, Iterable)` is False due to `__getattr__` specifically, to reduce the risk of false positives for mock/proxy objects used in unrelated contexts.

findings.description: The condition now reads `(isinstance(data, Iterable) or hasattr(data, "__iter__"))`. Because `collections.abc.Iterable`'s `__subclasshook__` itself just checks for the presence of `__iter__` on the class (effectively the same thing `hasattr` checks when `__iter__` is defined normally), the `isinstance` check is redundant for every case except objects that expose `__iter__` only via instance-level `__getattr__` delegation (the case this PR targets). The `or` adds a second, slightly more expensive check that is only ever needed, making the condition harder to read without actually broadening behavior beyond what `hasattr(data, "__iter__")` alone already covers.
findings.suggestion: Simplify to just `if not isinstance(data, (str, bytes, list, tuple, Mapping)) and hasattr(data, "__iter__"):` (dropping the now-redundant `isinstance(data, Iterable)` check), matching the pattern already used elsewhere in this module (e.g. `_encode_params`/`_encode_files`).

findings.description: The new test only exercises the fixed behavior through a full redirect-following HTTP round trip (`httpbin`), which is good for an integration-level check but doesn't directly unit-test `PreparedRequest.prepare_body`'s new condition in isolation (e.g. verifying `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` is set, or that `super_len`/body position logic behaves correctly for the `__getattr__` proxy). There is also no regression test confirming that Mapping/dict-like objects that implement `__getattr__` (and would now also pass `hasattr(data, "__iter__")`) are still correctly excluded via the `Mapping` isinstance check.
findings.suggestion: Add a focused unit test that calls `PreparedRequest().prepare_body(data=AttrProxy(), files=None, json=None)` directly and asserts `Transfer-Encoding` header / body assignment, plus a case for a dict-like `__getattr__` proxy that should NOT be treated as a stream, to pin down the exact boundary conditions independent of network behavior.

summary: This PR fixes a regression/edge-case where request bodies wrapped in proxy objects that only expose `__iter__` through `__getattr__` delegation (rather than defining it directly on the class) were not recognized as iterable/streamable, because `isinstance(data, collections.abc.Iterable)` relies on a class-level `__subclasshook__` check that doesn't see instance-level `__getattr__` fallbacks. Adding `or hasattr(data, "__iter__")` restores duck-typed detection consistent with how `_encode_params`/`_encode_files` already perform this check elsewhere in the same module, and a redirect-following functional test is added to demonstrate the fix. The change is small and sensible, but the `isinstance(data, Iterable)` branch is now largely redundant and the broadened `hasattr` check could introduce false positives for dynamic-attribute objects (e.g., mocks/proxies) that aren't truly iterable. Test coverage could be tightened with more targeted unit tests of `prepare_body` itself.

findings.description: The diff fixes a real correctness bug in Digest Auth response computation for the no-qop case (previously duplicated HA1, producing an invalid digest per RFC 2617), but no test changes are included in this PR to cover this specific scenario.
findings.suggestion: Add a unit test that exercises DigestAuth against a challenge without a `qop` directive and asserts the computed `response` value matches the RFC 2617 reference computation (`H(HA1:nonce:HA2)`), to prevent regressions of this bug.

summary: The PR changes the construction of `digest_data` in the Digest Auth implementation for the no-`qop` case, removing the duplicate `HA1` entry. Based on RFC 2617, when `qop` is not specified the response digest should be `H(HA1 ":" nonce ":" HA2)`. Since the surrounding code later computes `digest(b":".join((HA1, key_digest)))` (prepending `HA1` again), the previous code effectively produced `H(HA1 ":" HA1 ":" nonce ":" HA2)`, which is incorrect per the RFC and would cause authentication failures against servers that omit the `qop` directive. The fix correctly removes the redundant `HA1` from `digest_data`, so the final digest is `H(HA1 ":" nonce ":" HA2)`, matching the spec. This appears to be a legitimate bug fix with no apparent new issues in the diff. The main gap is a lack of accompanying regression test to verify the no-qop case produces the correct digest value and to prevent future regressions.
